question: What is the main reason we give packed red blood cells to a patient?

options.B: To boost white blood cell counts
options.D: To correct low serum albumin levels

explanation: You've got this! Packed red blood cells are packed with hemoglobin, which acts like little transport buses carrying oxygen from the lungs to every corner of the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do we treat a blood transfusion with the same high level of caution as an organ transplant?

options.A: It requires permanent immunosuppressive drug therapy
options.B: It can only be performed in major surgical theaters
options.C: It involves the total replacement of the patient's blood
options.D: It involves transferring living tissue that triggers immune responses

explanation: Think of donated blood as living tissue! When it enters a new body, the recipient's immune system will check it out and can spark a reaction if it doesn't match. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal donor for red blood cells?
explanation: Type O is a true lifesaver! Its red blood cells don't have A or B antigens on them, so recipient antibodies won't panic and attack them. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the main goal of cross-matching blood before a transfusion?

options.A: To determine the exact hemoglobin level of the donor blood
options.B: To detect any active reaction between donor cells and recipient serum
options.C: To warm the blood to body temperature before it leaves the lab
options.D: To check if the donor has a history of infectious diseases

explanation: Cross-matching is like a compatibility test in a tube. We mix the patient's blood with the donor's to make sure they play nicely together before it ever reaches the vein! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which IV cannula size is usually best when starting a blood transfusion for an adult?
explanation: Red blood cells are delicate! Using a nice wide-bore needle (like an 18G or 20G) prevents those precious cells from getting squashed or destroyed as they travel through the tubing. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h3)

question: You are getting ready to hang a unit of blood and notice your patient has a mild fever. What is your best first step?

options.A: Administer ice packs to reduce the temperature and infuse quickly
options.B: Report the fever to the physician before starting the transfusion
options.C: Cancel the transfusion entirely without notifying the doctor
options.D: Proceed with the transfusion and give paracetamol afterward

explanation: Always loop the doctor in! Since fever is also a top sign of a transfusion reaction, we need a baseline check so we don't confuse a pre-existing fever with a reaction later. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h3)

question: Which IV fluid is the only safe choice to use for priming blood tubing?
explanation: Stick to Normal Saline (0.9%)! Dextrose can actually make red blood cells burst (hemolysis), and Ringer's Lactate has calcium that can cause the blood to clot in the tubing. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why must a single unit of blood be completely infused within a maximum of four hours?

options.A: To prevent bacterial multiplication in the blood product at room temperature
options.B: To allow the nurse to finish the shift before the bag is empty
options.C: To ensure the patient does not become bored during the procedure
options.D: To prevent the blood from freezing inside the intravenous tubing

explanation: Blood is kept cold for a reason! Once it sits at warm room temperature for too long, bacteria love to multiply in it, which can put the patient at risk for severe infection. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the very first thing you must do if you suspect your patient is having a transfusion reaction?

options.B: Collect a urine sample for testing

explanation: Safety first! Stop the infusion right away to keep any more of that mismatched blood from entering their system. Every second counts. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which of these is a classic sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Lower back pain and dark urine
options.B: Dry cough and sudden hair loss

explanation: When red blood cells break down rapidly inside the body, the released hemoglobin travels to the kidneys and bloodstream, leading to classic flank/lower back pain and dark, tea-colored urine. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h5)

question: What complication is a patient most at risk for if they receive many blood transfusions over several years?
explanation: Our bodies are great at using iron, but terrible at getting rid of excess iron! Over years of multiple transfusions, that extra iron starts piling up in vital organs like the liver and heart. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why might a patient show signs of a delayed transfusion reaction a few days after getting blood?

options.A: The patient forgot to take prescribed post-transfusion antibiotics
options.B: Low-level antibodies increased over time and attacked newly introduced cells
options.C: The blood bag was stored in a refrigerator that was too cold
options.D: The intravenous cannula was left in place for too many days

explanation: Sometimes antibodies are so low in number that lab tests miss them initially. Once exposed to the donor cells, those antibody levels rise and start a delayed attack. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h6)

question: What should you do with empty blood bags right after a transfusion finishes?

options.A: Throw them into the general municipal waste bin immediately
options.B: Wash them out with soap and return them to the patient bedside
options.C: Burn them in the hospital incinerator within five minutes
options.D: Retain them temporarily according to institutional policy

explanation: Hang onto them for a bit! If the patient shows any delayed reaction, the blood bank might need those empty bags and tubing to run investigation tests. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why is it so important to accurately chart the exact time and volume of a blood transfusion?

options.A: It provides a legal record of care and helps track fluid balance
options.B: It prevents the patient from receiving another transfusion ever again
options.C: It is only required for hospital billing and insurance purposes
options.D: It allows the nurse to claim overtime payment for the procedure

explanation: Good charting keeps your patient safe and protects your license! It gives a clear picture of their fluid status and serves as a legal record that you delivered safe, quality care. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T12#GNS311_U2_T12_h7)
